lesson.title: sich & the Lost Reflexives
lesson.subtitle: hie thee hence, help yourself — the pronouns English dropped, German kept working

hook.title: Hie Thee Hence
hook.content: Shakespeare's English bounces actions back at the doer constantly: Get thee to a nunnery. Hie thee hence. Sit thee down. That thee is the reflexive pronoun doing its ancient job — and modern English keeps the fossils if you know where to look: help yourself, behave yourself, enjoy yourself. German never retired the system; it just standardized the pronoun: sich. ich wasche MICH, du wäschst DICH, er wäscht SICH, wir waschen UNS. The secret that makes it easy: the reflexive pronoun is just the ordinary pronoun from the Him-Case — except in the third person, where German deploys one all-purpose shape, sich, for he, she, it, they, and the formal Sie.

footnotes.title: The Feeling Verbs Are Reflexive by Birth
footnotes.content: sich freuen (rejoice — froh, the frolic family) and sich fühlen (feel) have no object: the feeling lands on the feeler. German makes that visible with sich; English hides it inside the verb. Ich freue mich = I glad myself = I am glad.

pattern.title: The Mirror Table
pattern.content: ich → mich (I wash myself: ich wasche mich). du → dich (thou thee! du wäschst dich). er/sie/es → sich. wir → uns. ihr → euch. sie (plural) → sich. Sie (formal) → sich. So only two new shapes exist: sich (third person + formal) and euch (ihr). Everything else you already drilled in the accusative gym. The stem-changer warning: waschen shifts a→ä in du and er — du wäschst dich, er wäscht sich. And reciprocal sich: Wir treffen uns — we meet (each other); Sie treffen sich — you (plural/formal) meet. Same pronoun, mutual action.
pattern.linguist_note: sich is the old dative/accusative reflexive *sik, shared with Old English (selfne / sīc in the Northumbrian glosses). English replaced it with self-phrases; Dutch and German kept the bare form. 'Himself' is literally the fossil: him + self, pronoun plus self glued together.

exercises.prompt: The mirror table — match each reflexive sentence with its reading. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: ich wasche mich, du wäschst dich, er wäscht sich, wir fühlen uns gut, sich freuen, Wir können uns erinnern, Wir können das erklären, Wir können gut verdienen, Wir können das bezahlen, Wir können beginnen, Das ist verboten, Wir können uns waschen
exercises.meaning: I wash myself; you wash yourself; he washes himself; we feel good; to rejoice / be glad; We can remember; We can explain that; We can earn well; We can pay for that; We can begin; That is forbidden; We can wash ourselves
exercises.explanation: The reflexive is the ordinary accusative pronoun — except third person, where everyone shares sich. The factory verbs next door (verdienen, bezahlen, beginnen) carry no mirror: they act on the world, not the self.

exercises.prompt: Third person shares one shape: 'Er freut _____.' (He is glad):
exercises.meaning: Er freut sich = he is glad (he rejoices himself)
exercises.explanation: er, sie, es, sie (plural) and Sie all take sich — the one reflexive pronoun German never splits.

exercises.explanation: du wäschst, er wäscht — the a→ä umlaut you know from the plural lesson (Mann → Männer), riding into the reflexive routine.

summary.outcome: Use the reflexive pronouns mich/dich/sich/uns/euch with waschen, freuen, fühlen and treffen.

use_example.german: Ich fühle mich gut und freue mich.
use_example.english: I feel good and I am glad.

summary.takeaway: The reflexive is your accusative pronoun bounced back — mich, dich, uns — with sich covering he/she/it/they/Sie.

erinnern.etymology_derivation: er- (out/thorough) + innern (inner) — to 'internal-ize' a thing; built on inn(inner), the twin of English inner. [wiktionary]

freuen.etymology_derivation: froh (glad) + -en — froh from Old High German frō, Proto-Germanic *frawaz 'quick, glad'; the English relative is frolic, borrowed from Dutch vrolijk 'joy-ly'. Reflexive: sich freuen. [wiktionary]

fühlen.etymology_derivation: Old High German fuolen, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan 'to feel' — the exact twin of English feel (Old English fēlan). Reflexive: sich fühlen. [wiktionary]

treffen.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → ff (cognate with English "drap" / strike).

uns.etymology_derivation: The accusative/dative of wir — the same West Germanic pronoun as English us. [wiktionary]

verdienen.context_translation: She earns a lot of money.
verdienen.etymology_derivation: From ver- + dienen (to serve), a calque of Latin deservio - the same Latin verb that gave English deserve (via Old French deservir). [wiktionary][etymonline]

beginnen.context_phrase: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
beginnen.context_translation: The film begins at eight o'clock.
beginnen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *biginnaną; the page documents cognate English begin — an exact class 3 ablaut twin: began and begann, begun and begonnen. [wiktionary]

bezahlen.etymology_derivation: be- + zahlen — the inseparable prefix at work on the tale-family verb. [wiktionary]

fieber.context_translation: The child has a high fever.
fieber.etymology_derivation: Borrowed early from Latin febris — English fever shares the same Latin source via French. [wiktionary]

vielleicht.etymology_derivation: Middle High German vil līchte 'very easily' — its second element is the ancestor of leicht. [wiktionary]

fröhlich.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz: froh 'cheerful' + the suffix -lich. [wiktionary]

uniform.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French uniforme, from Latin uniformis (uni- one + forma form); English uniform is the same borrowing. [wiktionary]

einige.context_phrase: Einige Leute warten vor dem Kino.
einige.context_translation: Some people are waiting in front of the cinema.
einige.etymology_derivation: Inflected form of einig, from ein (the exact twin of English one, Proto-Germanic *ainaz) plus the -ig suffix; some, a few. [wiktionary]

angeln.context_translation: My grandpa is fishing at the lake.
angeln.etymology_derivation: To fish with an Angel (fishing rod, hook) - the same old word as English angle, which survives in angler. [wiktionary]
